title: Courtroom Reversal
subtitle: 逆轉公堂 · Historical bilingual edition (pilot)
summary: As a fictional modern lawyer, students investigate the Yang Naiwu and Xiaobaicai case (1873–1877) in three short chapters. They collect records from the Board of Punishments' 1877 memorial, press testimony, and present evidence at the statement it contradicts. Then they choose a closing assessment that says no more than the record supports. It makes them argue about whether matching or repeated statements can count as proof.
game_form: Courtroom visual novel: investigation, pressing testimony, presenting evidence
region: Yuhang and Hangzhou, Zhejiang, Qing China
social_topology: One player per device; a pair can share one screen
sources_rights: The main source is the Board of Punishments' case-settlement memorial of Guangxu 3/2 (1877), a Qing government text in the public domain. The game uses the simplified-character Wikisource transcription, archived on 2026-09-25; it may contain errors and has not been checked against an archival facsimile. The courtroom background and the character sprite sheets come from the earlier, novel-based version of this game. That version's notice calls its characters, script and art 'adapted and generated by this project' (本專案改編與生成) and limits use to non-commercial teaching, research and display. The source repository names no licence for the code or the art, and this edition does not add one. The sound cues are made in the browser; there are no recordings.

human_tests.note: This listing links to a website, so students need the internet to open it. The game is a folder of files (index.html plus an assets folder), not one HTML file. The source project's own browser test opens the packaged folder from disk with the browser set offline and plays all three chapters (tests/playthrough.py, lines 286-302); a local log dated 2026-10-09 says it passed. That was an automated script, not a person, and the log is not kept in the repository's history.

All controls are native buttons and selects, and the stylesheet draws a visible focus outline (assets/pilot.css, line 55). The README says keyboard users can tab through the buttons (README.md, lines 33-34). But the browser test drives the game with mouse clicks and only presses Escape to close dialogs. Nobody has played it with the keyboard alone.

The opening screen says 'About 20-30 minutes' (assets/campaign-content.js, line 17). That is the author's estimate, not a timed run. session_minutes adds about 15 minutes of briefing and debrief to the upper figure. Nobody has timed a class.

Not opened on a classroom computer, a projector, or through an LMS. An agent only checked that the live site loads and a case starts (test ledger row 12). Saves are kept per browser, so a shared room computer will offer the last student's 'Resume case'.

An automated test checks that all twelve Chinese quotations in the game appear word for word in the local copy of the memorial, and that the copy matches its recorded SHA-256 hash (tests/content.test.cjs, lines 20-26). An agent re-ran it on 2026-10-13 and it passed. That does not check the English translations or the Traditional Chinese explanations, and it does not check the Wikisource copy against an archival facsimile. No historian has read the Sources & glossary screen against the memorial.

The game has no debrief questions. Each chapter ends with a short note on what the objection does and does not establish, and the final screen has a section called 'The limits of vindication'. The teacher guide offers six suggested questions, drafted by an agent from the game's content. No instructor has reviewed them or used them in class.

provenance_note: Built on one source: the Board of Punishments' 1877 case-settlement memorial on the Yang Naiwu and Xiaobaicai case, from a Wikisource transcription brought over from the author's qing_court_game research collection. Twelve short Chinese excerpts are quoted in their original simplified characters and are checked by a test against a local copy of that transcription. The English translations and Traditional Chinese explanations were written for this game. The lawyer Cheng Yilong, all spoken dialogue, the three compressed hearings, and the player's access to later records are invented teaching devices, and the game labels them as such. The art and the lawyer character come from an earlier version of the game based on a late Qing novel; that version's plot (the magistrate's son as murderer, a forged pharmacy ledger) is not used.

title: Many Centres, One World
subtitle: A map quiz of the great voyages, c. 1400–1600
summary: Students find 24 ports, mines and capitals on a world map, from Zheng He's fleet at Liujiagang to the silver mountain at Potosí, then trace five trade connections. The rounds start in East Asia, not Lisbon, and the game ends by asking why the usual 'Age of Discovery' story starts in Europe.
game_form: Map quiz: four pins per question, five rounds
region: World: East Asia, Indian Ocean, Southeast Asia, Mediterranean, Atlantic, Africa, the Americas
social_topology: Individual copies on students' own laptops
license: The instructor owns the game. Cited sources keep their own terms.
sources_rights: No source text is reproduced beyond short facts; every explanation is written new and cites its sources. The world outline is Natural Earth (public domain). Wikipedia is cited by fixed article versions (CC BY-SA). Britannica and UNESCO pages are cited, not copied.

human_tests.note: An agent opened the file from disk in headless Chromium with the network switched off and played all 29 questions to the end. No network request was made and no error appeared. No person has tried it with the wifi off.

An agent played the whole game with Tab and Enter only, from the opening screen to the final map, and checked where the focus went after every screen change. Visible focus was checked in screenshots, not by a person. No screen reader was tried.
Nobody has timed a real play-through. There are 29 questions; the game says 'about 15 minutes'. The 25 minutes includes a short briefing and the debrief, and is an estimate.
Not opened on a classroom computer, a projector or through an LMS.

An agent found and read every source and spot-checked five facts again, but no historian has checked the 29 answers against the sources. Eight items rest on Wikipedia alone; the History Bible lists them.

Five debrief questions are shown on the final screen and in the teacher guide. They ask students to criticise the game itself: its choice of places, its round order, its map centre, what a point rewards, and whose experience a map of ports leaves out. No instructor has used them yet.

provenance_note: Built with an AI agent (Claude) on 13 October 2026 for an instructor who asked the agent to find the sources. The agent read about 59 sources (Ming History biography of Zheng He, UNESCO World Heritage pages, Britannica, and fixed versions of Wikipedia articles) and wrote every question and explanation from them, citing each. Nothing is invented. Three items are marked contested (Malindi, Columbus's landfall, how much silver reached China). Eight items rest on Wikipedia alone. No historian has checked it yet.

title: The Yang Naiwu Case
subtitle: 楊乃武案 · A wrongful conviction in Qing China, 1873–1877
summary: Play a real Qing homicide case in six short chapters: as the county magistrate at the inquest, as the family appealing to the capital, as the commissioner at the retrial, and as an official of the Board of Punishments reviewing the whole file. Students pick passages from the 1877 memorial, the Code and the Shenbao as evidence, and argue how a wrongful conviction was made, step by step.
game_form: Case-file reading and courtroom review in six chapters (Godot web game)
region: Yuhang and Hangzhou, Zhejiang; Beijing; Qing China
social_topology: One player per computer. The design documents do not describe group play.
sources_rights: The game quotes Qing official documents (the Board of Punishments memorial and the edicts of 1877, the Veritable Records of the Guangxu Emperor, a Censorate memorial of 1874), Shenbao reports of 1874–1875, the Great Qing Code, Collected Cases of Injustice Rectified (洗冤集錄) and Wang Huizu, all through Wikisource transcriptions that the source project records as public domain. Code articles also come from Kyoto University's electronic text of Xue Yunsheng's Duli cunyi; the project records the old text as public domain and the electronic edition as Kyoto University scholarly material. The epilogue quotes a 2013 newspaper article (short quotation only). The Chinese Wikipedia article (CC BY-SA 4.0), a modern novel and Alford's 1984 article are used as a basis, not quoted. The 33 pictures are AI-generated or made for the game, and are labelled in the game as imagined, not historical sources. Fonts: Noto Serif TC and Noto Sans TC, SIL Open Font License 1.1. The author has not stated a licence for the game itself.

human_tests.note: This is a hosted game, not a single file. It is a Godot web export (about 49 MB of files) served from GitHub Pages, and it needs the internet every time it loads. It cannot be opened with the wifi off. Nobody tried to make it work offline.

The project's automated test plays the whole of chapter 4 with Tab and Enter only, and checks after every key that the focused control is fully visible, at 1280×800 and at 1024×640 with 200% text. It ran as part of the full test suite, which passed on 2026-10-10. It runs inside the Godot engine, not in a web browser, and covers chapter 4 only. Separately, on 2026-09-25 an agent drove an early version of the web build in Chrome by keyboard only (title, chapter, reader, language switch). No person has played the game by keyboard, and the other five chapters have no whole-chapter keyboard test.

The design plans a 90-minute class: about 60–65 minutes of play (chapter times add up to 65) plus about 30 minutes for briefing and discussion. The design says the times will be adjusted after a trial. Nobody has timed a play-through, and the student trial in the design has not happened.

No classroom computer, projector or LMS has been tried. An agent loaded the public site in Chrome from a clean browser cache after each publish on 2026-09-25 and 2026-09-26 and saw it load with no console errors, and checked the current build at 1440×900 at 2× scaling on 2026-09-27. That shows the site works, not that it works on your room's machine and network. Thirty students loading about 18 MB each at once has not been tried.

No person has checked the game's source labels and its Credits and sources screen against the documents. AI agents did a lot of checking: a script confirms every quotation matches the downloaded source text exactly, and an AI agent (GLM) checked the history of each chapter. But in the project's own records, 10 of 32 historical claims are still marked 'draft' (the game shows them as 'Not yet checked'), every English translation is still 'draft', and the project's release check fails on these sign-offs (883 items, journal entry of 2026-10-10).

The game's teacher materials have two or three discussion questions for each of the six chapters (13 in all), copied into teacher-guide.md in Chinese and English without the answers. But this check asks for 3–6 questions that make students criticise the game as an interpretation of the past, and none of the 13 does that. Only the epilogue's two questions (legend against archive) ask how the case is told. Add such questions before counting this check as done.

provenance_note: Built by AI agents for Kwok-leong Tang between 25 September and 10 October 2026: GLM-5.3 searched for and downloaded sources, Claude led and wrote the code, Codex reviewed the code and design. Almost every quotation comes from the Board of Punishments' memorial of 1877 (88 of 163 quoted passages); the rest are from edicts, the Veritable Records, the 1874 petition to the capital printed in the Shenbao, other Shenbao reports, the Great Qing Code and Collected Cases of Injustice Rectified. A script checks each quotation against the downloaded text. The texts are modern Wikisource transcriptions with some OCR errors, and the Code text is a 1905 edition, not the one in force in 1873–1877. Two documents are reconstructed and labelled as such, one witness line is labelled an inference, and the player's choices inside each chapter are counterfactual: each chapter returns to the real history at the end. All pictures are imagined. The English is a draft translation. No person has reviewed the history.

title: The Influenza Front Page
subtitle: Newsroom edition
summary: Edit a retrospective front page of Philadelphia's Evening Public Ledger from eighteen readings of October 3-10, 1918, with three or six research checks to spend and exactly six columns to fill. Then meet the October 12 mortality figures and qualify, replace, or defend one story.
game_form: Newsroom page-building with a staged archive
social_topology: Teams of three or four on one device; solo; or two independent pages for a debate
license: CC BY 4.0 for the game layer (code, rules, readings, and other text). The newspaper crops are public domain and are not covered by this licence
sources_rights: The eight newspaper crops are from 1918 issues of the Evening Public Ledger in the Library of Congress Chronicling America collection (LCCN sn83045211). They are public domain: the Library describes these newspapers as public domain or having no known copyright restrictions. Consult each item's rights statement before reuse. The game's readings are editorial paraphrases, not transcriptions.

human_tests.note: Opened as a file:// URL in Chrome on 2026-09-14; the page loaded no resources beyond itself. The game's own Playwright suite, re-run the same day, also checks for network requests during a full play-through and found none. That suite is not included in this repository, so its result cannot be reproduced from here.

The game's Playwright keyboard test was re-run on 2026-09-14 and completed a full game with Tab, Enter, Escape, and typed text only, including dialog focus restoration. That test is not included in this repository, so its result cannot be reproduced from here. On 2026-09-24 an agent drove one stage of the recompressed file by keyboard in Chrome (see test-ledger.md). No person has played it by keyboard.

The teacher guide gives a sixty-minute lesson plan and a forty-minute variant; session_minutes is the full sixty-minute lesson. The in-game How to play stage times now match that plan. Nobody has timed a class.
No classroom setup to test against. The guide asks instructors to rehearse the exact file on the classroom browser and to download rather than preview it in an LMS.

An audit on 2026-09-07 checked eight of the eighteen readings and the reveal against the embedded newspaper crops and corrected five figures. The other readings are labelled in the game as not independently checked. Nobody has re-read the Sources screen against the Library of Congress pages since.

The ending screen has descriptive indicators, an exportable editorial record, and a panel called Hold the editorial conference with five questions about the team's own page. The teacher guide has a separate set of six whole-class questions and a feedback rubric; students do not see those in the game.

provenance_note: Built from a single newspaper, Philadelphia's Evening Public Ledger, October 3 to 12, 1918, via the Library of Congress. Eighteen editorial readings and eight page crops are embedded. The readings are AI-assisted paraphrases, not diplomatic transcriptions; an audit against the crops corrected five numbers and the history bible says exactly which readings were checked and which were not. The newsroom, the column budget, the research checks, and the staged release of sources are teaching models, not a reconstruction of any editorial meeting.
